newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU may move to restrict plant relocations.
newsitem.headline: EU may move to restrict plant relocations.

text.p: Spurred by Renault's controversial decision to close down a car plant in Belgium, the European Commission may well try to regulate relocations if it suspects firms want to use subsidies to switch operations from high to low-labour cost regions within the 15-nation EU.

Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert reacted angrily on Thursday to a Spanish request to have permission to grant France's Renault SA 11 million European currency units ($12.4 million) in aid to increase production at its plant in the northern town of Valladolid.
"It is obviously absurd that one may be able to close a profitable company and invest in Spain with public money," an outraged Van Miert told Belgian radio.
Van Miert added that he would block the Spanish aid unless Renault management changed its attitude on the closure of the plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels.

His spokesman later tried to play down the comments saying they meant the Commission would carefully scrutinise the Spanish request to make sure Renault was not moving to Spain simply to take advantage of state subsidies.
But it was clear that the Commission is trying to clamp down on a growing trend to relocate production centres in EU regions where labour costs are cheaper and incentives higher.

According to a recent study by the German car association VDA, Spanish and British car workers cost respectively 28 ($16.5)and 27 marks per hour compared with 44.6 marks in Belgium and 62.4 marks in Germany -- where automobile labour costs are the highest.

Spain, Britain and Portugal have traditionally benefited from foreign investment because of their cheaper labour costs. One famous example was the decision by British household appliances firm Hoover to close its operations in the French town of Angers and move production to Scotland.
National authorities and the Commission have been unable to counter what most see as unfair competition. But the Commission seems to believe it has a case with Renault.
"They will have to prove that the investment could not be carried out anywhere else," Van Miert's spokesman told reporters.
"If this is about moving jobs within the group to shop for subsidies, is it logical?," another official close to Van Miert said.
Lawyers well versed in European competition law agree it may not be fair, but they doubt whether the Commission can intervene in such commercial decisions.
"We are talking about unchartered waters. But I'm certainly sceptical as to the legallity of such a move," one lawyer said.

Renault's announcement last week that it would close its Belgian factory in Vilvoorde sparked angry protests from Van Miert's native country Belgium, where prospects of finding new jobs for over 3,000 workers are slim.
The Spanish request came only a few days later, in what looked like confirmation that the French move was dictated by the desire to reduce costs at the expense of Belgian workers.

The Commission cannot block an aid request without first investigating whether it is compatible with EU rules and, in this particular case, with rules on aid to the car industry. This could take several months during which the plan is effectively on hold.

In assessing such plans, it normally takes into account the development of the region where aid is to be paid. It will also carry a cost-benefit analysis of the investment project. Most importantly, the Commission will check that public money is not being used to increase overall capacity in the European car industry estimated to exceed demand by some two million vehicles.

Valladolid is situated in the Castille-Leon province, one of the EU's poorest regions. This means subsidies can amount for as much as 40 percent of the total investment which in the Renault case is valued at 76 million Ecus.
